group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 66-year-old man presented this afternoon to the multidisciplinary pre-operative medicine clinic at the request of the neurosurgery service six days before a scheduled elective L4–L5 decompressive laminectomy with instrumented fusion intended to alleviate neurogenic claudication that has limited him to walking less than one city block despite maximal medical management; the operating surgeon expects the procedure to last roughly two and a half hours in the prone position under general anesthesia with postoperative admission to the regular surgical floor for one night of observation and early ambulation under physical-therapy guidance. The patient drove himself, parked in the adjacent garage, and walked the length of the corridor with a rolling backpack but no assistive device, stopping once to stretch because of leg numbness rather than breathlessness. He reports that he routinely mows a small lawn on a riding tractor, climbs a single flight of household stairs several times daily without pausing, and swims leisurely laps for twenty minutes twice a week at the community center; he sleeps on a single pillow, has not awakened short of breath, and denies paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, ankle swelling, orthopnea, exertional chest pressure, palpitations, or dizziness. Past medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed nineteen years ago when fasting glucose exceeded 200 mg/dL; oral agents controlled values for a decade, but rising glycated hemoglobin led his endocrinologist to initiate basal-bolus therapy five years ago. He currently administers insulin glargine 34 units subcutaneously at bedtime and rapid-acting insulin lispro according to a 1:10 gram carbohydrate ratio before meals with a correction factor of 1 unit for every 25 mg/dL above 150; electronic glucometer downloads reviewed at a primary-care visit last week showed most fasting readings between 110 mg/dL and 160 mg/dL and no hypoglycemic episodes requiring assistance. Hypertension was diagnosed in midlife and is treated with lisinopril 20 mg each morning and amlodipine 5 mg nightly; home blood-pressure logs average 122/70 mm Hg. Hyperlipidemia is managed with rosuvastatin 20 mg. Stage 4 chronic kidney disease, attributed to long-standing diabetic nephropathy, was recognized three years ago when serum creatinine first exceeded 2.0 mg/dL; nephrology follow-up occurs every six months, and no dialysis access has been planned. He denies history of swollen legs, elevated jugular venous pressure, cardiomyopathy, myocardial infarction, coronary intervention, stroke, transient neurologic deficits, carotid imaging, or peripheral arterial revascularization. Surgical history consists only of a remote cholecystectomy performed laparoscopically without complication. He quit cigarette smoking twenty-five years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks one bottle of light beer with weekend dinner, and denies recreational drug use. Family history reveals a father who died of renal failure at 78 and a mother alive with insulin-treated diabetes; no first-degree relatives suffered early cardiac or cerebrovascular events. Review of systems today is negative for fever, cough, orthostatic light-headedness, abdominal pain, claudication, or unintentional weight change beyond a deliberate five-pound loss after dietitian counseling. After five minutes of seated rest, vital signs taken in the right arm were blood pressure 118/66 mm Hg, regular pulse 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97 % breathing ambient air, and oral temperature 36.7 °C; body mass index is 29 kg/m². The patient appeared comfortable and well nourished. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was nondisplaced in the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line. Heart sounds were crisp with physiologic splitting of S2 and no S3, S4, murmurs, or rubs. Lungs were clear to auscultation throughout with good air entry bilaterally. Abdominal examination revealed well-healed periumbilical laparoscopic scars, no palpable organomegaly, and normoactive bowel sounds. Extremities were warm with 2+ radial and dorsalis pedis pulses and no edema or calf tenderness. Neurologic evaluation showed intact cranial nerves, full motor strength except for pain-limited dorsiflexion of the right great toe, symmetric deep-tendon reflexes, preserved sensation to light touch and vibration, and a steady tandem gait when not limited by back discomfort. Laboratory studies drawn one hour prior to the visit demonstrated hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, white blood cells 7.2 × 10⁹/L, platelets 256 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, chloride 101 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, and a serum creatinine of 2.6 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 25 mL/min/1.73 m²; fasting plasma glucose in the same sample was 132 mg/dL, and hepatic enzymes, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, and international normalized ratio were within reference limits. Twelve-lead electrocardiography obtained today showed normal sinus rhythm at 70 beats per minute with normal intervals, axis, and no ST-segment deviations compared with a tracing from the prior year. Upright posterior–anterior chest radiograph displayed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Airway assessment by anesthesia revealed a Mallampati class II view, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, and full cervical extension. The intra-operative plan includes continuation of the morning angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitor, withholding the evening basal insulin dose by 25 %, omitting prandial insulin while nil per os, hourly capillary glucose checks, balanced crystalloid at restricted rate to mitigate fluid overload in the setting of reduced renal clearance, and avoidance of non-steroidal analgesics post-operatively. Mechanical thromboprophylaxis, incentive spirometry, early ambulation, and nephrology consultation for postoperative medication dosing were reviewed; the patient affirmed understanding, voiced no additional questions, and expressed readiness to proceed with the scheduled spine surgery.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative findings:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): lumbar decompression and fusion is none of these = 0.
- Ischemic heart disease: no documented coronary disease, prior infarction, or angina = 0.
- Heart failure: no history or clinical evidence of heart failure = 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA = 0.
- Diabetes treated with insulin: uses glargine and lispro = 1.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: preoperative creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL = 1.
Total = 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 2.
Final answer: 2
